title: Disabled Veteran property tax homestead exclusion
summary: North Carolina excludes the first $45,000 of appraised value of your permanent residence from property tax if you are a Veteran with a VA certified permanent and total service-connected disability. An unremarried surviving spouse can qualify too.
amount: The first $45,000 of appraised value of the residence is excluded from taxation
eligibility: Your character of service at separation was honorable or under honorable conditions
And the VA or another federal agency has certified that, as of January 1 before the tax year, you have a service-connected, permanent, and total disability
Or you had received benefits under 38 U.S.C. 2101 as of that January 1
Or the Veteran is deceased and the VA certified that the death resulted from a service-connected condition
You are a North Carolina resident and an owner of the permanent residence
An unremarried surviving spouse of a disabled Veteran also counts as a qualifying owner
There is no income limit written into this particular exclusion
details: The statute directs you to file during the regular listing period, but applications must be accepted at any time up to and through June 1 preceding the tax year for which the exclusion is claimed. Do not wait past June 1.
You apply through your county tax office, not the state. Counties administer the listing period and process the paperwork.
You have to submit either a copy of the Veteran's disability certification or evidence of the benefits received under 38 U.S.C. 2101.
A married couple who own and occupy the home together get the full exclusion even if only one of them qualifies.

You do not lose the exclusion by being away temporarily for health reasons, or by an extended stay in a rest home or nursing home, so long as the residence is empty or lived in by your spouse or another dependent.
Co-owners who are not married to each other each have to apply separately. Each qualifying co-owner gets the full exclusion, capped at their proportionate share of the property's value.
A qualifying owner receiving this exclusion cannot also receive the other property tax relief programs in Chapter 105, so compare before you choose.
agency: North Carolina Department of Revenue, administered by county tax offices

title: Deduction for military retirement pay and Survivor Benefit Plan payments
summary: North Carolina lets you deduct military retirement pay from your state taxable income if you served at least 20 years or were medically retired. Survivor Benefit Plan payments to a beneficiary of an eligible retiree are deductible too.
eligibility: You receive retirement pay from the United States government for service in the uniformed services
The statute uses the definition of uniformed services in 10 U.S.C. 101(a)(5), which reaches beyond the Armed Forces to the commissioned corps of the Public Health Service and of NOAA
And you served at least 20 years in the uniformed services, or you were medically retired under 10 U.S.C. Chapter 61
Severance pay for separation under 10 U.S.C. Chapter 61 does not qualify
A beneficiary receiving payments from a plan defined in 10 U.S.C. 1447, the Survivor Benefit Plan, can deduct them if the retired member met the conditions above
The deduction is only allowed to the extent the payments are included in your adjusted gross income
details: This deduction applies to taxable years beginning on or after 1 January 2022.
There is no cap. North Carolina deducts the whole qualifying amount, which is a meaningfully better deal than the capped subtractions in states like Virginia and California.
The 20 year threshold is the catch. A retiree with 19 years and a non-medical separation does not qualify at all, and there is no partial deduction.

This is separate from the older Bailey settlement deduction under G.S. 105-153.5(b)(5) for certain federal, state, and local retirement benefits. The statute says the same amount cannot be deducted under both, so if you are a Bailey-protected retiree, work out which one applies before filing.
The deduction is claimed on your North Carolina return. It is not automatic.
amount: The full amount of qualifying retirement pay. The statute sets no dollar cap.

title: North Carolina Scholarship for Children of Wartime Veterans
summary: North Carolina awards scholarships to the children of Veterans who were killed, disabled, held as prisoners of war, or listed missing in action. The award is worth eight academic semesters, and you have eight years to use them.
amount: Eight academic semesters, usable within eight years
eligibility: You are under 25 years of age at the time you apply
You are a resident of and domiciled in North Carolina when you apply
You have completed high school or its equivalent before receiving the scholarship, and have complied with Selective Service requirements if they apply to you

Your Veteran parent was a legal resident of North Carolina when entering the period of service that establishes eligibility, or you were born in North Carolina and have lived here continuously since birth
You meet the definition of child in 37 U.S.C. 401

Your Veteran parent falls into one of the statutory classes: killed in action or died of service-connected causes, rated 100 percent for a wartime service-connected disability, rated 20 percent or more but less than 100 percent or awarded a Purple Heart, deceased or drawing a nonservice-connected permanent and total disability pension or having served in a combat zone or a campaign with an authorized badge or medal, or listed as missing in action, captured, or forcibly detained
details: There is an escape hatch on the birth requirement that families do not know about. If you were not born in North Carolina, the Department may still waive that requirement where your mother was a native-born North Carolina resident, was a resident when she married the Veteran, was temporarily outside the state when you were born, and you were brought back to North Carolina within a reasonable time and have lived here since.
The statute sorts awards into Class I-A, I-B, II, III, and IV. Class II and Class III are each capped at 100 children per year. The other classes are not capped.

Class III is the broadest and the one most post-9/11 families fit: it covers a Veteran parent who served in a combat zone or adjacent waters, or in any campaign, expedition, or engagement for which the Department of Defense authorizes a campaign badge or medal. It is one of the two classes limited to 100 awards a year, so apply early.

Class I-B is a limited award, but it upgrades itself. If the Veteran parent later dies of the wartime service-connected condition before the recipient has used all their eligibility time, the Department amends the award from Class I-B to the fuller Class I-A for the remainder.
You may be considered under more than one class, but you can only be awarded one scholarship.
The Persian Gulf War period in the statute begins 2 August 1990 and has no end date yet, because it ends only on a Presidential proclamation or a concurrent resolution of Congress.

At a North Carolina public institution the program pays allocable costs including room, board, and tuition. At an approved private institution it instead pays a fixed monetary allowance per academic term, with a lower rate for Class I-B. Confirm the current allowance figures with the Department before you rely on them.

The deadline is 14 February for the classes covering a Veteran rated less than 100 percent service connected or who served in a combat zone. Other classes have separate deadlines. As of August 2026 the Department has closed the portal for the Fall 2026 semester, so the next opening is the one to watch.
Applications are filed on the Department's scholarship portal, not with the college. Paper applications are obsolete and are returned to sender.
agency: North Carolina Department of Military and Veterans Affairs

title: In-state tuition rate for Veterans and their dependents
summary: A Veteran using federal education benefits can pay the North Carolina in-state tuition rate and mandatory fees at a public college without waiting out the usual 12 month residency period, as long as North Carolina is their home and they file a letter of intent to establish residence.
eligibility: You completed active duty of not less than 90 days in the Armed Forces, the Commissioned Corps of the US Public Health Service, or NOAA, and were discharged or released from that service
You qualify as a covered individual under 38 U.S.C. 3679(c), which also reaches certain dependents using transferred benefits
Your abode is in North Carolina
You give the institution a letter of intent to establish residence in North Carolina
The waiver runs to the extent required by 38 U.S.C. 3679, so the federal rule sets its outer edge
details: This route skips the standard 12 month durational residency requirement that other students must meet, and it covers applicable mandatory fees, not tuition alone.
The statute puts the burden of proof on the person applying, so bring your DD-214 and your VA certificate of eligibility to the residency determination.

A separate statute, N.C.G.S. 116-143.3, gives the in-state rate and mandatory fees to a qualifying federal services member whose permanent duty station is in North Carolina, and to that member's dependents.

That one keeps paying after the assignment ends. If the member is reassigned out of state or retires, the member and the dependents stay eligible so long as they remain continuously enrolled in the same program. If the member is on active duty and receives an honorable discharge, they stay eligible by establishing North Carolina residency within 30 days of discharge and staying continuously enrolled.
A dependent child who lives with an Armed Forces member reassigned outside North Carolina also keeps eligibility under the same statute.
agency: University of North Carolina System and the North Carolina Community College System

title: Military and Veteran license plates with no additional plate fee
summary: North Carolina issues a long list of military and Veteran special registration plates, and the fee table sets the additional special plate charge for them at none. You still pay the ordinary registration fee.
amount: No additional special plate fee beyond the regular registration fee
eligibility: 100% Disabled Veteran plate: issuable to a Veteran of the Armed Forces who suffered a 100 percent service-connected disability
Partially Disabled Veteran plate: issuable to a Veteran who suffered a service-connected disability of less than 100 percent
Military Veteran plate: issuable to an individual who served honorably in the Armed Forces, and it shows the branch insignia
Purple Heart Recipient plate: issuable to a recipient of the Purple Heart award
Prisoner of War plate: issuable to a member or Veteran member of the Armed Forces who was captured and held prisoner by forces hostile to the United States while serving
details: The statutory fee table lists an additional fee of none for Active Member of the National Guard, Bronze Star Recipient, Bronze Star Combat Recipient, 100% Disabled Veteran, Ex-Prisoner of War, Gold Star Lapel Button, Legion of Merit, Legion of Valor, Military Veteran, Military Wartime Veteran, Partially Disabled Veteran, Pearl Harbor Survivor, Purple Heart Recipient, and Silver Star Recipient.
The disabled Veteran and Purple Heart plates are available for motorcycles as well as motor vehicles.
The plate statutes do not by themselves grant a disabled parking placard or waive the regular registration fee. Ask NC DMV about those separately.
agency: North Carolina Division of Motor Vehicles

title: Resident Disabled Veteran Lifetime Sportsman License
summary: A North Carolina resident Veteran rated 50 percent or more disabled by the VA can buy a lifetime hunting and fishing sportsman license for a one-time fee of $100. It is good for the rest of your life.
amount: $100.00 one time, for a lifetime license
eligibility: You are a resident of North Carolina
You are a 50 percent or more disabled Veteran as determined by the United States Department of Veterans Affairs
details: The license covers taking wild animals and birds by lawful methods other than trapping during open seasons, plus hook-and-line fishing in inland waters and public mountain trout waters.

The statute also creates a Resident Totally Disabled Lifetime Sportsman License at the same $100 fee for a resident who is totally and permanently disabled as determined by the Social Security Administration.
These are inland privileges. Coastal recreational fishing is licensed separately.

title: Veterans preference in North Carolina state government employment
summary: North Carolina gives eligible Veterans a hiring preference for state jobs covered by the State Human Resources Act. Military training and additional service count toward the qualifications for the job.
eligibility: A Veteran who served during a period of war
A Veteran who suffered a service-connected disability during peacetime
The spouse of a disabled Veteran, and the spouse of a Veteran disabled during peacetime
The surviving spouse or dependent of a Veteran who dies on active duty during a period of war, directly or indirectly as a result of that service
The surviving spouse or dependent of someone who served on active duty for reasons other than training and died for service-related reasons during peacetime
Veteran means a person who served on active duty for reasons other than training and was discharged under other than dishonorable conditions
details: Read the period of war definition before you assume you are outside it. The statute lists World War I, World War II, the Korean Conflict, and the stretch from 31 January 1955 to the end of hostilities in Vietnam on 7 May 1975, and then adds "any other campaign, expedition, or engagement for which a campaign badge or medal is authorized by the United States Department of Defense." That last clause is what carries most post-Vietnam service.

There is a separate National Guard preference under N.C.G.S. 126-80.5 that this record does not otherwise cover. It reaches a current North Carolina Army or Air National Guard member in good standing, a former member discharged under honorable conditions with at least six years of creditable service, and the surviving spouse or dependent of a member who died on state active duty or for service-related reasons during peacetime.

The preference applies to positions subject to the State Human Resources Act with every state department, agency, and institution. It reaches initial employment as well as subsequent hirings, promotions, reassignments, and horizontal transfers.

The State Human Resources Commission must give credit for all military service training or schooling and experience that bears a reasonable and functional relationship to the job's requirements. Once you clear the minimum requirements, you also get experience credit for additional military service, related or unrelated.
In a reduction in force where seniority or years of service is one of the retention factors, the Commission may allow an eligible Veteran credit for military service.
If you believe you were denied the preference, you can appeal. N.C.G.S. 126-82(d) points to the contested case procedures in 126-34.01 and 126-34.02.
The statute has teeth. Willful failure by a covered state employee to comply with this Article is personal misconduct, and the chapter's rules for suspension, demotion, or dismissal apply.
Some categories of positions are excluded. Check N.C.G.S. 126-83 for the exclusions before you count on the preference for a specific posting.
agency: North Carolina Office of State Human Resources

title: Burial in a North Carolina State Veterans Cemetery
summary: North Carolina provides a free burial plot and interment services in a state Veterans cemetery for a qualified Veteran. A spouse and certain dependents can be buried there too, but a burial fee applies to them.
amount: No charge for the gravesite or necessary interment services for a qualified Veteran. A burial fee applies for an eligible spouse or family member.
eligibility: Any former member of the US Armed Forces who served on active duty and was discharged under honorable conditions
A Veteran entitled to retired pay for non-regular service in the Reserve Components or the Army or Air National Guard, or who would be entitled but for being under 60 years of age
The spouse, widow, or widower of a qualified Veteran
Unmarried minor children under 21, or under 23 if enrolled in an approved course of education
An unmarried adult child who became permanently disabled before age 18
details: The state covers the burial plot, opening and closing the grave, the marker and its installation, and perpetual care for a qualified Veteran.
All funeral expenses stay the responsibility of the Veteran, the family, or the estate.

The DD Form 214 is the primary document used to verify honorable service. Reserve and National Guard members claiming eligibility through non-regular service present a 20 year letter or proof of retired pay eligibility.
If you cannot find your DD-214, a county or state Veterans service officer can help you get a replacement copy.
agency: North Carolina Department of Military and Veterans Affairs

title: North Carolina State Veterans Homes skilled nursing care
summary: North Carolina runs State Veterans Homes that provide skilled nursing care, therapy, and on-site help from Veterans Service Officers. The homes are state licensed and approved for Medicare, Medicaid, and third party insurance.
eligibility: The state page does not publish the admission requirements. Call the department or a Veterans Service Officer to find out whether you qualify and what the cost would be.
details: The department lists State Veterans Homes at Black Mountain, Fayetteville, Kernersville, Kinston, and Salisbury.
Care is provided by registered nurses, licensed practical nurses, and certified nursing assistants under the direction of licensed physicians, with a registered dietician and social work support.
Physical, occupational, and speech therapy are provided in the facility, along with therapeutic recreation programs and community outings.
Veterans Service Officers work on site and help residents apply for VA benefits.
Hospital care is arranged through VA medical centers or local hospitals.
The department lists a toll free number, 844-624-8387, to reach a Veterans Service Officer.
agency: North Carolina Department of Military and Veterans Affairs
